title: Modeling the side brace
content:
Below the arm of the Airline Chair, a straight wooden brace runs from the front leg to the back end of the arm, where it fits into the notch you left in Part 2 and is held by a small metal bracket. In this part you'll model the brace and the brackets as separate objects, each a stretched cube with supporting edges and a Subdivision Surface modifier, then line the brace up with the side. You'll need the side from Part 2 and the reference image. The video uses Blender 2.83.

Model the brace

  1. Study the reference. 0:00 The photos don't show this piece clearly: it may get a little thicker or wider, and the lighting doesn't help. It's basically a rectangle that's been extruded, so it goes quickly 0:21.

  2. Add a cube and stretch it. 0:28 In Object Mode, press Shift+A and choose Mesh → Cube. Press S to scale it down, then S, Y to stretch it along Y 0:38. Don't add the cube while you're in Edit Mode on the side, or it becomes part of the side's mesh 0:50.

  3. Shape it flat, over the reference. 0:43 Go back to the Right Orthographic view and turn on X-ray. If it helps, hide the side by clicking its eye icon in the Outliner 0:55. Press Tab and move the brace's ends and edges into place over the photo. The brace is flat, so model it level, in its ideal form, rather than at the angle it sits at: you can rotate it into position later 1:13.

  4. Level the reference to suit. 1:27 Add a couple of edge loops with Ctrl+R where the thickness changes, and bring the thickness down if it's too high. To keep the brace level, the video rotates the reference back slightly (its rotation is unlocked, changed and locked again), then moves the brace up into place 1:53. Moving the reference isn't usually a good idea; later you'll rotate the brace to fit the side instead 7:31.

  5. Set its width. 2:16 Show the side again. You can eyeball the width, or look from the front (Front Orthographic) and scale the brace along X (S, X) so it sticks out a little on each side of the side piece 2:28. It doesn't have to be exact.

  6. Add control edges. 2:40 Hide the side again. To make the shape you want, add two edges to each face. Press Ctrl+R and scroll for two loops, then scale them apart with S, X towards the edges 2:50. Do the same the other way with Ctrl+R and S, Z 2:58. For the last direction, place the loops by hand 3:04.

  7. Adjust it with X-ray on. 3:10 Back in the side view, press 1 and pull down the vertices that need it. Without X-ray, you only select the vertices in front, so turn it back on and select them again 3:25.

  8. Smooth it. 3:33 Add an edge loop to hold the corner that needs to be tighter. Choose Shade Smooth: even without a modifier it looks good. Then add a Subdivision Surface modifier and set it to 3 3:47. The shape stays square, but the bevel catches a highlight, which makes all the difference when you texture and render it later. Pull the shape a little further if it needs it, and add a supporting edge to hold it 4:14. Then save.

Model the brackets

  1. Add a thin cube. 4:45 Add another cube, scale it down, then scale it along X until it's quite thin, and move it back along Y (G, Y) to the bracket in the photo 4:56. Press Tab and move its vertices to match the bracket's outline.

  2. Choose which corners stay round. 5:10 Use the same principle as on the other pieces: add edges to tighten the curves you want to stay square when it's subdivided. In one direction, leave them off completely: with a Subdivision Surface modifier at 3, that direction rounds off because nothing is holding it 5:29. Add supporting edges in the other direction, using the scroll wheel for two loops and scaling them along X 5:53. If it's too thick, press A and scale it 6:10.

  3. Place it against the brace. 6:33 The bracket sits on the outside of the brace. Look at the brace end-on (the video shows it in Back Orthographic) and move the bracket in until it's just touching, the way it would be built in real life 6:45.

  4. Make a linked copy for the other side. 6:55 Press Alt+D: it duplicates like Shift+D, but makes an instance, so a change to one bracket changes them all. Press X to constrain the move to the X axis and put the copy on the other side of the brace 7:05.

Fit the brace to the side

  1. Check how the pieces line up. 7:18 Show the side again. Because the reference was rotated to model the brace flat, the brace doesn't quite line up with the side: it needs to be rotated back a little 7:45. Select the brace and both brackets and move them into place with G 8:00.

  2. Move the origin to the pivot point. 8:10 The brace needs to be rotated up slightly, from its back end, but objects rotate around their origin, the little dot in the center. In the header, open Options and, under Transform → Affect Only, tick Origins 8:20. Now moving changes only the origin: move it to where you want to rotate from. Then untick Origins again 8:30.

  3. Rotate the brace into place. 8:32 Press R and rotate the brace up a little so it lines up with the side.

  4. Edit it in its local orientation. 8:41 If the brace isn't quite far enough forward, change the Transform Orientation to Local: in Edit Mode, moving then follows the object's own orientation, not the global one, so you can edit it as if it weren't rotated. That keeps it intact: if you set its rotation back to 0 later, it's still perfectly straight, as if you'd modeled it in the side view 8:55.

  5. Check the result. 9:14 Orbit around and make sure the brace is in position against the side.

Wrap-up

You've modeled the brace and its brackets from cubes, using supporting edges to choose which corners stay square and which round off, and you've made the second bracket a linked duplicate. You moved an object's origin to rotate it from the right place, and edited it in its local orientation so its shape stays true. Next, you'll mirror the side to make the other side of the chair.
